items.q: In triangle ABC, a = 12, A = 60°, B = 45°. Find b.
hints: Use the sine rule: a/sin A = b/sin B.
sin(45°) = sqrt(2)/2, sin(60°) = sqrt(3)/2, so b = 12sqrt(2)/sqrt(3) = 12sqrt(6)/3 = 4sqrt(6)

items.q: In triangle ABC, a = 10, b = 14, A = 35°. Find angle B (to the nearest degree).
items.imageAlt: Triangle ABC. Side a (opposite A) is 10, side b (opposite B) is 14, and angle A is 35 degrees. Angle B is unknown.
hints: Use the sine rule sin(A)/a = sin(B)/b, rearranged to find sin(B).
sin(B) = b x sin(A) / a = 14 x sin(35°) / 10.

items.q: Two sides of a triangle are 5 cm and 7 cm with included angle 60°. Find the third side.
items.imageAlt: Triangle ABC. Side AC is 5 cm, side AB is 7 cm, and the included angle A between them is 60 degrees. The third side, BC, is unknown, marked a.
hints: Use the cosine rule: c² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C.

items.q: Two sides are 8 cm and 10 cm with included angle 90°. Find the third side.
hints: Use the cosine rule: c² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C.
c² = 164, so c = sqrt(164) = sqrt(4 x 41) = 2sqrt(41)

items.q: Two sides are 12 cm and 5 cm with included angle 180°. Find the third side.
hints: Use the cosine rule: c² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C.
c² = 169 + 120 = 289, so c = sqrt(289) = 17 (a 180° angle means the sides lie in a straight line, so the third side is just their sum: 12 + 5)

items.q: A triangle has side a = 10, angle A = 30°, and side b = 12. How many possible triangles are there?
items.imageAlt: From vertex A, angle A is 30 degrees and side b is 12. A circle of radius a (10) centred at the far end of b crosses the base ray from A at two points, giving two possible triangles.
items.imageCaption: Two triangles fit: AB₁C and AB₂C.
hints: Find h = b sin A, then compare it with a.
h = 12 x sin(30°) = 6; since h < a (6 < 10) and a < b (10 < 12), there are two possible triangles.
Two triangles: one with angle B acute, one with angle B obtuse.

items.q: A triangle has side a = 8, angle A = 45°, and side b = 5. How many possible triangles are there?
hints: Compare side a with side b first.
Since a ≥ b (8 ≥ 5), there can only be one possible triangle.
When the side opposite the given angle is at least as long as the other given side, only the acute case works — one triangle only.

items.q: A triangle has side a = 6, angle A = 30°, and side b = 14. How many possible triangles are there?
items.imageAlt: From vertex A, angle A is 30 degrees and side b is 14. Side a is 6, too short for the swing to reach the base ray, so no triangle is possible.
items.imageCaption: No triangle: the swing never reaches the base.
hints: Find h = b sin A, then compare it with a.
h = 14 x sin(30°) = 7; since a < h (6 < 7), no triangle is possible.
Zero triangles — side a is too short to reach the base line.

items.q: A triangle has side a = 9, angle A = 35°, and side b = 11. How many possible triangles are there?
hints: Find h = b sin A, then compare it with a.
h = 11 x sin(35°) ≈ 6.31; since h < a (6.31 < 9) and a < b (9 < 11), there are two possible triangles.
Two triangles: one with angle B acute, one with angle B obtuse.

items.q: A triangle has side a = 7, angle A = 60°, and side b = 6. How many possible triangles are there?
items.imageAlt: From vertex A, angle A is 60 degrees and side b is 6. Side a is 7. Since a is at least as long as b, only one usable triangle results.
items.imageCaption: Only one triangle fits: a ≥ b.
hints: Compare side a with side b first.
Since a ≥ b (7 ≥ 6), there can only be one possible triangle.
When the side opposite the given angle is at least as long as the other given side, only the acute case works — one triangle only.

items.q: A triangle has side a = 5, angle A = 20°, and side b = 9. How many possible triangles are there?
hints: Find h = b sin A, then compare it with a.
h = 9 x sin(20°) ≈ 3.08; since h < a (3.08 < 5) and a < b (5 < 9), there are two possible triangles.
Two triangles: one with angle B acute, one with angle B obtuse.
